summary:
Legal gender recognition in Andorra rests on the 2022 Law of the Person and Family, which allows trans people to update name and gender on legal documents through a simple process that requires no medical intervention. The same legislation unified civil marriage, so a trans visitor's marital status is recognised under the same regime as everyone else's.

Statutory non-discrimination protection covers gender identity and expression. Law 13/2019 of 15 February 2019 bars discrimination on grounds including gender identity and expression across employment, education, health care, social services, housing and public establishments, and extends that protection specifically to education settings. Law 14/2019 of 15 February 2019 on the rights of children and adolescents establishes that transgender children must be respected in their gender identity. Bias-motivated offences attract additional penalties under the Penal Code, and expression-related bias is penalised alongside bias on sexual orientation.

Enforcement remains thin. Andorran police recorded an average of two to three bias-motivated incidents each month during 2025, according to ILGA-Europe's most recent annual review. No formal system exists to register and classify bias-motivated violence; DiversAnd, the country's principal LGBTI organisation, has called for one so that such incidents can be recognised as hate crime, which indicates that the generic hate-crime provisions of the Penal Code are not routinely applied to bias incidents of this kind. DiversAnd flagged incidents around the June Pride celebrations of 2025 and reported them publicly. The Ministry of Equality implemented equality measures during that year and obliges companies operating in the country to maintain protocols against sexual and gender-based harassment.

Access to gender-affirming care is a live question rather than an established entitlement. In August 2023 DversAnd met the Ministry of Health to press for gender-affirming protocols covering puberty blockers and hormone therapy for 16-year-olds, and in some cases 14-year-olds, following the 2022 regulatory changes. Whether the ministry adopted those protocols is not established in the sources.

Public bias in the media has drawn a documented institutional response. A transphobic opinion piece published in El Periòdic d'Andorra on 27 September 2023 was removed online with a public apology after DiversAnd requested its removal, though it had already run in print.
tangentialFactors:
Andorra's head of government, Xavier Espot Zamora, who has held office since 2019, came out as gay publicly in September 2023, stating "I never hid it". He remains the serving prime minister, which is a signal about the societal climate a trans visitor will encounter, though it says nothing directly about legal protections.

Public LGBT expression is protected and has a visible history: the first LGBT demonstration was held on 6 September 2002 and the first gay pride parade followed on 23 June 2003 at Plaça del Poble in Andorra la Vella, organised by the association Som Com Som. DiversAnd was formed in 2019 after Som Com Som ended its work in 2018, and organised a pride parade in June 2019; on 17 May 2019 the Department of Equality launched the short film "#lovingdiversity" to raise online awareness.

Violence against LGBT people has a documented history in the country. In 2000 a 17-year-old gay man, Nuno Ribeiro, was murdered because of his sexual orientation, prompting public outcry, and cases of parents expelling their children from home over their sexual orientation are also reported. These are LGB-specific and historical rather than trans-specific, but they bear on the risk environment.

GayLawNet's Andorra page indexes civil unions, discrimination, hate crimes, marriage, sodomy and trans legal status, and sets the age of consent at 16 under Penal Code Article 206; the page carries a "limited information" marking, so it should not be treated as an authoritative statement of current law.
localsOnly:
Adoption has been open to same-sex couples since the 2014 civil union law, and the 2022 family law consolidated marriage for same-sex couples. These are resident-facing family-law provisions rather than entry or visitor questions.

Preventing and addressing bullying and discrimination in schools is a stated focus of DiversAnd, and Law 13/2019 extends non-discrimination protection including gender identity and expression to education settings, while Law 14/2019 governs the treatment of transgender children by reference to their gender identity.

Employers operating in Andorra are required by the Ministry of Equality to maintain protocols against sexual and gender-based harassment, a workplace obligation that falls on residents and staff rather than on short-term visitors.

The age of consent is 16 for both same-sex and heterosexual relationships under Penal Code Articles 162 and 163, and same-sex sexual activity has been legal since the prohibiting law was abolished in 1791.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Ministry of Health adopted gender-affirming protocols covering puberty blockers and hormone therapy for 16-year-olds, or in some cases 14-year-olds, following the August 2023 meeting with DiversAnd is unresolved in the sources; the advocacy request is documented, the outcome is not.

Whether the police figures of two to three bias-motivated incidents per month during 2025 break down by protected characteristic, and how many involved gender identity rather than sexual orientation, is not sourced. Nor is it established whether the Penal Code's hate-crime enhancements have been applied in any specific trans-related case.

GayLawNet's Andorra page carries a "limited information" marking, so its statement of the age of consent and its index of trans legal status should be verified against the primary legislation before use.
